tldr: By training a visual planner and a whole-body tracker separately on whole-body human motion data collected without a robot, this study achieves dynamic, contact-rich humanoid manipulation including kicking and climbing on a real robot.
hero_caption: A real Unitree G1 humanoid performs advanced whole-body tasks: crouching low to carry boxes to a shelf, kicking a third box into place with its foot, catching a thrown box mid-air, and toppling and climbing onto a suitcase.
overview:
For humanoid robots to work flexibly like humans, manipulating objects with their arms alone is not enough. They must also perform dynamic whole-body motions—crouching low, bracing against or kicking objects with their feet, and stepping up onto obstacles (whole-body loco-manipulation). However, relying solely on egocentric RGB cameras and proprioceptive joint sensors to plan and execute contact-rich, disturbance-resistant whole-body motions in real time has been an extremely difficult challenge.

To address this, the authors propose Workhorse, a framework that learns tasks directly from human whole-body demonstrations recorded without a robot. The core idea is to adopt a spatial pose interface of five links—the torso, both wrists, and both feet—as the shared language between human and robot. Without retargeting human motions to robot joint angles, the raw five-link trajectories from human demonstrations serve both as target predictions for a visual planner and as tracking commands for a reinforcement-learning whole-body tracker. Furthermore, custom data augmentations are introduced to imitate the prediction errors and tracking discrepancies that inevitably arise at deployment, yielding a robust system where both policies compensate for each other's mistakes.

In real-robot experiments on a Unitree G1, Workhorse successfully achieved contact-rich tasks: sorting boxes onto a shelf and kicking a final box in, catching a thrown box, and pushing over a suitcase to climb onto it as a stepping platform. The robot recovers and continues its task even when pushed, kicked, or when a box is snatched away by a person. Moreover, the exact same human demonstrations were used to retrain policies for a different, larger humanoid (Unitree H2), demonstrating high versatility and robustness.
contributions: Built a lightweight capture setup that records contact-rich whole-body manipulation without a physical robot, using only five wearable trackers and a chest camera.
Trained a visual planner and a whole-body tracker separately using a shared 5-link pose interface (torso, wrists, feet) without retargeting to robot joint angles.
Introduced data augmentations and image editing that simulate deployment latency, errors, and external disturbances, enabling the planner and tracker to absorb each other's mistakes and self-recover.
Demonstrated kicking, climbing, and disturbance recovery on a real robot, and verified that skills transfer to a humanoid with a different morphology using the same demonstration data in simulation.

sections.heading: Toward Robots That Engage the World with Their Entire Body
sections.summary: To thrive in human environments, humanoid robots must coordinate their entire bodies, using their legs not just for locomotion but also as manipulation tools to kick objects or step onto platforms. Workhorse achieves robust whole-body motion from an egocentric perspective using robot-free human data and a 5-link pose interface.
sections.details:
Humans naturally crouch deeply when lifting heavy boxes, brace with their legs to push obstacles over, or climb onto platforms to reach high places. While research in humanoid imitation and reinforcement learning has advanced whole-body motion, much of it has been limited to tracking predefined whole-body reference trajectories. Planning and controlling dynamic whole-body motions in real time from only egocentric camera views and proprioceptive sensing, adapting to constantly shifting environments, has remained a formidable hurdle.

One common approach to teaching robots whole-body tasks is teleoperation using physical robots. However, this requires the robot hardware, skilled human operators, and often suffers from restricted operational interfaces that hinder fast, dynamic movements. Conversely, robot-free approaches capture human motion with wearable sensors, but previous works have treated legs almost exclusively as a means of walking, failing to support dynamic actions where legs act as manipulation tools or quickly recover from strong external disturbances.

Workhorse overcomes this barrier. Human tasks are recorded without a physical robot using wearable trackers and a camera, with the spatial poses of five links—the torso, both wrists, and both feet—acting as a shared bridge. Because the method eliminates motion retargeting to robot joint angles, natural human movements directly serve as training targets.

sections.heading: How Workhorse Reinvents Whole-Body Control, Data Capture, and Imitation
sections.summary: This section reviews three lines of prior work—whole-body humanoid controllers, human data collection hardware, and policy learning from demonstrations—and highlights how Workhorse distinguishes itself. Key differences lie in its task-space interface design that avoids retargeting and training strategies that anticipate deployment-time prediction discrepancies.
sections.details:
### II-A Humanoid Whole-Body Controllers
Many controllers track whole-body reference trajectories, but most treat retargeted motions or teleoperation inputs as ground truth. In reality, when a visual planner updates its plan online, commands drift over time and jump discontinuously whenever replanning occurs. Workhorse trains its reinforcement-learning whole-body tracker to handle these anticipated drifts and jumps from the outset.

### II-B Human Data Collection Hardware
Optical motion capture is accurate but bulky and expensive. Wearable inertial measurement units (IMUs) suffer from positional drift over time. Lightweight devices like UMI rely on wrist camera odometry, but extending them to whole-body tracking requires five cameras including the feet, introducing time synchronization issues and tracking failures on the ground. Workhorse uses four base stations and five wearable trackers to track the torso, hands, and feet simultaneously in a single gravity-aligned coordinate frame, yielding a lightweight and reliable capture system.

### II-C Humanoid Policy Learning from Human Demonstrations
Imitation learning for humanoids typically retargets human poses into robot joint angles. However, retargeting is tied to a specific robot morphology and distorts the original human motion. Workhorse uses the recorded 5-link spatial poses directly as training targets for both policies. As a result, deploying to a different robot requires no new demonstrations—only retraining policies from the same recorded data.

sections.heading: Recording High-Quality Whole-Body Demos Without a Robot
sections.summary: The data collection setup accurately records human movements and egocentric video during tasks using just five wearable trackers and a chest-mounted action camera. Real-time inverse kinematics verifies that the human's reach stays within the robot's workspace, while a three-clap gesture aligns video and tracker timelines with millisecond accuracy.
sections.details:
### III-A Capture Rig Setup
The capture hardware is remarkably simple. Five HTC Vive trackers are mounted on the chest camera rig, the backs of both hands, and on both shoes. These are tracked by four Lighthouse base stations at $60\,\mathrm{Hz}$ in a single, gravity-aligned world frame. Egocentric video is recorded at $30\,\mathrm{fps}$ using a DJI Osmo Action 4 mounted on the chest, capturing wide-angle, near-fisheye footage. Because the real robot mounts the exact same camera on its chest, video can be used directly without distortion correction.

### III-B Recording Protocol and Real-Time IK
In each recording session, demonstrators insert a "T-pose" between task repetitions to facilitate episode segmentation. Crucially, inverse kinematics (IK) for the robot is solved in real time as the demonstrator moves, previewing on a screen whether the human hands exceed the robot's physical reach. If an out-of-reach error occurs, the demonstrator immediately adjusts their posture, preventing unreachable demonstrations from entering the dataset. While object poses are varied to provide diversity, demonstrators themselves are never pushed or obstructed, capturing only clean, intentional motions.

### III-C Synchronization and Data Processing
Because the camera and trackers run on independent clocks, the demonstrator performs three claps at the start of each recording. An audio-motion score—matching tracker distance and velocity peaks against audio peaks recorded by the camera microphone—automatically identifies the time offset. After synchronization, residual timing error is only $5.5\,\mathrm{ms}$. Tracker trajectories are then resampled to $50\,\mathrm{Hz}$ to match the control frequency of the whole-body tracker.

captions.F3: The real-time IK preview screen used during data collection. The system continuously verifies whether the robot model can solve the pose, displaying a warning if hand tracking error exceeds a 5 cm threshold so the demonstrator can immediately adjust their stance.

sections.heading: Bridging Human 5-Link Poses to the Robot: Coupling the Two Policies
sections.summary: This section details how the visual planner and whole-body tracker are separately trained and integrated around the 5-link pose interface. Key elements include image editing that swaps human arms for robot arms in first-person video, data augmentations that build resilience against tracking drift and disturbances, and timestamp management to smoothly couple the asynchronous policies.
sections.details:
### IV-A 5-Link Pose Interface
The interface connecting human and robot consists of five link poses: torso, both wrists, and both feet. By specifying poses in task space rather than joint space, the interface remains independent of robot kinematic structure and degrees of freedom. By simply composing fixed frame offsets on the human wrists and shoe soles with those on the robot's corresponding links, recorded human poses directly become the robot's target poses.

### IV-B Visual Planner Architecture and Data Augmentation
The visual planner takes a 4-frame history of egocentric RGB images and recent 5-link poses to predict a future $1.16\,\mathrm{s}$ (58-step) 5-link target trajectory, implemented using a Flow Matching policy and a Diffusion Transformer. Two gaps arise between demonstrations and real deployment: human arms appear in the video, and real-world disturbances cause the robot's pose history to drift from ideal trajectories.

To resolve these gaps, an offline pipeline segments human arms using SAM 3, inpaints the background with LaMa, and overlays simulated robot arms using depth estimates from MoGe-2. Additionally, "drift augmentation" applies random-walk translational and rotational drift to the pose history while warping input images accordingly. This ensures that even when the robot is knocked off course, the planner remains oriented and generates valid recovery trajectories.

### IV-C Whole-Body Tracker and Command Augmentation
The whole-body tracker is a low-level reinforcement learning controller that tracks the upcoming $0.2\,\mathrm{s}$ of 5-link commands from the planner and outputs target joint positions. During training, "command augmentation" simulates command drift between $5\,\mathrm{Hz}$ planner updates and abrupt jumps upon replanning. The reward formulation tracks wrist poses in absolute terms while tracking foot poses relative to the torso, allowing the robot the flexibility to brace and maintain balance when pushed without being rigidly bound to foot commands.

### IV-D Real-Robot Deployment and Temporal Integration
The visual planner runs at $5\,\mathrm{Hz}$, while the tracker executes at $50\,\mathrm{Hz}$. By measuring sensor and inference latencies, all commands receive accurate timestamps. The tracker interpolates and executes commands valid from the current time onward, and incoming plans are in उन्हेंinpainted into previous trajectories to avoid jerky, discontinuous motions.

captions.F4: A Unitree G1 robot model overlaid onto a recorded human demonstration. By targeting task-space poses for the hands and feet without retargeting-based scaling, natural human crouching postures are intuitively preserved on the robot.
captions.F5: The visual planner's image-editing training pipeline. Human arms are removed from the recorded egocentric video and replaced with simulated robot arms rendered with accurate depth relationships, bridging the visual domain gap to real-robot camera feeds.

sections.heading: Kicking, Climbing, and Recovering: Real-Robot and Simulated Evaluations
sections.summary: On a real Unitree G1, Workhorse validates three dynamic tasks—box sorting with a kick, box catching, and suitcase climbing—demonstrating autonomous recovery when pushed or when objects are taken away. Extensive ablations in a realistic simulated environment confirm the importance of the proposed interface and augmentations.
sections.details:
### V-A Real-Robot G1 Whole-Body Manipulation
Real-robot experiments operated entirely without external motion capture, relying solely on the onboard camera and proprioceptive sensors.
- **Box Sorting and Kicking**: The robot walks to the boxes, crouches deeply to place two boxes onto a shelf by hand, and powerfully kicks a third box into the lower shelf with its foot. When kicked or pushed sideways by a person, the tracker recovers balance while the visual planner re-acquires the box. When a box is snatched away mid-task, the robot smoothly transitions to the next available box.
- **Catching a Thrown Box**: The robot visually tracks a box thrown toward it (airborne for roughly $0.56\,\mathrm{s}$), catches it in mid-air with both hands, and sets it on the floor.
- **Pushing, Toppling, and Climbing a Suitcase**: The robot pushes a wheeled $14\,\mathrm{kg}$ suitcase, uses its foot to topple it flat, steps up $0.39\,\mathrm{m}$ onto the suitcase, grabs a box from a high shelf, and steps back down.

### V-B Ablations in a Simulated Digital Twin
In a simulation reconstructed from the physical lab using 3D Gaussian Splatting (Polycam scan), the full system achieved a $77\%$ success rate across 100 box-sorting episodes without disturbances, and maintained $64\%$ success under strong $40\,\mathrm{N\cdot s}$ pelvis impulse disturbances.
- **Joint Angle Commands**: Replacing 5-link targets with 29-joint commands solved via online IK dropped success to $54\%$ without disturbances and $42\%$ with pushes, likely due to IK singularities and solver errors.
- **Link-Local Coordinate Frame**: Expressing targets relative to each link's current frame destroyed overall posture coordination, causing success to plummet to $5\%$/$4\%$ with frequent falls.
- **Removing Projected Gravity**: Omitting gravity alignment from the pose history reduced success to just $1\%$.
- **Data Augmentations**: Removing planner drift augmentation caused success under disturbance to collapse to $0\%$, while removing tracker command augmentation reduced disturbed success from $64\%$ to $52\%$ (with fall rates worsening from $15\%$ to $23\%$).

### V-C Skill Transfer to a Different Robot (Unitree H2)
Retraining policies for the full-sized Unitree H2 in simulation using the identical human demonstration dataset yielded an $83\%$ success rate without disturbances. This verifies that skills transfer across robot morphologies simply by swapping the robot model and retraining, without recollecting human data.

captions.F9: The simulation environment scanned and reconstructed using 3D Gaussian Splatting. Matching background textures and rendering at the exact field of view and resolution of the real camera enables high-fidelity closed-loop evaluation.

sections.heading: Current Limitations and Future Directions
sections.summary: Current limitations include task-specific policies, confinement to environments with tracking base stations, and the absence of dexterous fingers or neck degrees of freedom in the interface. Future avenues include richer whole-body representations and collecting data in unconstrained environments.
sections.details:
The authors highlight several limitations. First, separate planners and trackers are trained for each task rather than forming a single multi-task policy. Furthermore, demonstrations were recorded in a single room by a single demonstrator, retaining dependencies on the room's appearance and the demonstrator's body proportions.

Second, quantitative success rates are evaluated exclusively in simulation, leaving real-world statistical success rates unmeasured. Under simulated $40\,\mathrm{N\cdot s}$ disturbances, the robot still experiences a $15\%$ fall rate, indicating room for improved robustness against severe impacts.

Third, the 5-link interface omits finger grasping, multi-fingered hand kinematics, and neck movement (camera gaze control). Incorporating active visual search and dexterous manipulation requires expanding the interface. Finally, because tracking relies on Lighthouse base stations, extending data collection to outdoor or expansive environments remains an open challenge.

takeaways: Abandoning joint-angle retargeting in favor of a shared 5-link task-space interface (torso, wrists, feet) preserves natural human whole-body motions without distortion.
Decoupling the visual planner and whole-body tracker while training both with augmentations that simulate deployment drift and disturbances yields high real-world robustness and recovery.
Replacing human arms with robot arms in video and warping images alongside pose drift dramatically narrows the sim-to-real gap in egocentric imitation learning.
A single set of human demonstrations can transfer whole-body skills to humanoids of different body sizes simply by updating the robot model and retraining policies.
limitations: Separate planners and trackers must be trained for each individual task, rather than operating as a generalist multi-task policy.
Quantitative success rates are evaluated only in simulation; statistical real-world success and fall rates are not reported.
The 5-link interface excludes dexterous finger articulation and independent neck or gaze control.
Data collection is confined to laboratory environments covered by Lighthouse base stations.
